title: Registry
subtitle: The kitchen’s central freezer: a pencil label vs a fingerprint
mission: On Monday, Aunt Cida pushed api-pedidos 1.4 to the registry, and server A pulled it. On Tuesday, a teammate pushed 1.5 (and the latest tag moved with it). On Wednesday, server B is born and pulls the same reference A used. Compare deploying by version tag, by latest and by digest; and see what happens if someone re-pushes the 1.4 tag over the old one.

predict.question: server A pulled api-pedidos:1.4 on Monday. On Wednesday, B pulls api-pedidos:1.4 too, after the teammate pushed 1.5. What does B run?

feedback.right: right: pushing 1.5 doesn’t touch the 1.4 label, which still points to the same content. As long as nobody re-pushes over it… which, spoiler, is possible.
feedback.wrong: it’s 1.4. Each tag is a separate label: pushing 1.5 moves latest, but not 1.4. Both servers run the same digest.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run it and compare both servers’ digests.

coach.ui: guess noted. Run with the version tag, then switch to latest. Compare both servers’ versions.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run deploy and compare the versions on servers A and B.

tryNext.ui: Turn on "a teammate re-pushed 1.4": even a version tag is just a label. Then switch the reference to digest with the re-push still on.
tryNext.cmd: Run deploy --overwritten yes (even a version tag is just a label) and then deploy --ref digest --overwritten yes.

why.simples:
The registry is the kitchen’s central freezer: you store lunchboxes there and any branch picks them up. The label (tag) is written in pencil: “lasagna of the week” is one today and another next week, and someone can erase it and write again. The digest is the lunchbox’s fingerprint: if the content is different, the fingerprint is different.
latest is nothing magical: it’s just a label people usually stick on the newest lunchbox. Asking for “latest” means asking for “whichever has that label right now”.
why.dev:
An image’s full name: registry/path/repository:tag, like ghcr.io/escola/api-pedidos:1.4. With no registry in the name, Docker uses Docker Hub (docker.io), and official images live under library/: node:24-slim is docker.io/library/node:24-slim. On GHCR the name is ghcr.io/OWNER/IMAGE, and login uses a personal token (docker login ghcr.io). On ACR the name uses the registry’s login server (something like myregistry.azurecr.io; az acr create shows the exact loginServer), and login is az acr login --name myregistry.
A tag is a pointer that can move: docker push with an existing tag moves the pointer. A digest (sha256:…) is the manifest’s hash and never changes: name@sha256:… always brings exactly the same image.
why.especialista:
In production: push tags that never repeat (semantic version or the commit SHA), never reuse a version tag and deploy by digest. Several registries let you lock tags against overwrites (on ACR, by locking the image; on ECR, with immutable tags). latest is for experimenting, not deploying; in Kubernetes it also flips the imagePullPolicy default to Always.
A tag can point to a multi-platform index (amd64 and arm64), and the index digest differs from each manifest’s digest. The registry is also a security surface: sign images (cosign, Notation), generate an SBOM, scan for vulnerabilities and use machine credentials (managed identity on Azure, GITHUB_TOKEN in Actions) instead of personal passwords.

mission.ui: time to break it: deploy by the latest tag.
mission.cmd: time to break it: run deploy --ref latest

break.success: Broken: both servers asked for {fullRef}, but A runs {a} and B runs {b}. A label that moves doesn’t guarantee everyone runs the same code, and the bug that only shows up “on some servers” is born like this.
break.calm: A and B run {b}, asking for {fullRef}. To break it, deploy by the latest tag.

steps:
Start a local study registry (no TLS, for your machine only):
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:3
On macOS port 5000 may be taken by AirPlay; in that case use -p 5001:5000 and replace localhost:5000 with localhost:5001 in the next steps.

Give lesson 3’s image a name with an address and push it (the last push line shows the digest, sha256:…):
docker tag api-pedidos:1.0 localhost:5000/api-pedidos:1.0
docker push localhost:5000/api-pedidos:1.0

Ask the registry what it stores; it’s an HTTP API:
curl http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog
curl http://localhost:5000/v2/api-pedidos/tags/list

Delete the local label and pull by the digest from step 2:
docker image rm localhost:5000/api-pedidos:1.0
docker pull localhost:5000/api-pedidos@sha256:PASTE_THE_DIGEST_HERE
docker image ls --digests localhost:5000/api-pedidos
recipe.ok: _catalog lists api-pedidos, the tag list shows 1.0, the pull by digest finishes without errors and docker image ls --digests shows the same sha256 that appeared on push.
